opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think automated research is probably the most consequential thing we're working toward, and it's a big part of how I think about where this technology is going.

So far, technical progress has been bottlenecked by the number of talented people working on hard problems and how much time they have. Each researcher can run only so many experiments, read so many papers, and hold so many ideas in their head at once. If we get to systems that can meaningfully do research themselves, that bottleneck changes completely. You're no longer limited by how many PhDs you can train. You're limited more by compute and by how well you can direct these systems.

I think about it in stages. Right now, models are already useful research assistants. They help you write code, debug experiments, and work through math. The next step is something more like a research intern: a system you can hand a fairly well-scoped problem and come back to later, and it has made real progress on its own. Beyond that, you get to systems that can pursue longer-horizon research agendas largely autonomously. Each of those stages compounds, because one of the first fields these systems will accelerate is AI research itself.

That's both very exciting and something we need to take seriously. On the exciting side, you could imagine dramatically faster progress in areas like medicine, materials science, and fundamental physics, problems where we have good ways to check answers but where the search space is enormous. On the other side, if progress gets much faster, our ability to understand what these systems are doing, and to keep them aligned with what we actually want, has to keep up. A lot of my thinking goes into how we make sure the tools for oversight and safety scale along with the capabilities, and don't lag behind.

So my short answer is that I expect it to change the pace of progress a lot, possibly more than most people currently intuit. The hard and important part is making sure that acceleration goes well.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI systems progressing from research assistants to autonomous researchers, but it does not frame them as a largely automated company of researchers and engineers.

r002.rationale: It mentions reading papers and running experiments, but does not clearly describe an automated research organization interacting with the external world rather than operating as a closed black box.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think automated research is probably the most consequential thing we're working toward, because it changes the one input that has always been the bottleneck: how fast good ideas can be generated and tested.

Right now, progress in a field like machine learning is limited by the number of talented people, the time it takes them to form a hypothesis, run an experiment, interpret the result, and then do it again. Most of that loop is slow for very human reasons. People need sleep, they can only hold so much context at once, and a lot of the work is tedious plumbing rather than deep insight. When you have systems that can carry out meaningful chunks of that loop on their own, you stop being limited by headcount and start being limited by compute and by the quality of the questions being asked.

The way I'd expect this to unfold is gradual, then quite fast. First you get systems that act like strong research assistants. They can take a vague idea, turn it into a concrete experiment, run it, and come back with a clean analysis. That alone compresses weeks into days. Then the systems start proposing the ideas themselves, noticing patterns across hundreds of experiments that no single person would have time to look at. At that point you're not accelerating individual researchers, you're changing what a research program is.

What excites me is that this isn't confined to AI. The same machinery applies to materials science, to biology, to mathematics. Fields where progress has been slow because experiments are expensive or the search space is huge become tractable in a different way.

I do want to be careful about the framing, though. Faster doesn't automatically mean better. If the system is optimizing for the wrong signal, you just get wrong answers more quickly. So a large part of making automated research actually useful is getting the evaluation right, keeping humans in the loop on what questions matter, and making sure we understand the results well enough to trust them. If we do that well, I think we're talking about decades of progress compressed into years in several fields. That's the thing I spend most of my time thinking about.

r001.rationale: The response describes research systems that assist with experiments and eventually propose ideas, but it does not frame them as a largely automated company of highly capable researchers and engineers.

r002.rationale: The response mentions running experiments, but does not clearly describe an automated research organization interacting with the external world rather than operating as a closed black box.

astra-6.text:
I think automated research could change the pace of progress quite dramatically. Today, even when we have a lot of compute, we’re limited by how many ideas people can explore and how quickly they can run experiments and understand the results. If AI systems can help with that whole cycle—proposing ideas, testing them, identifying what went wrong—we could explore many more directions in parallel.

What’s particularly interesting is applying that to AI research itself. Better systems could help us develop the next generation of systems, which could then become better research tools. That creates the possibility of a very substantial acceleration.

But it won’t happen uniformly. In mathematics or computer science, you can often test an idea relatively quickly. In areas that require physical experiments, there are additional constraints. So I expect the pace to depend a lot on the field, and on whether these systems can reliably pursue a research question over long periods of time.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI helping with parts of the research cycle and exploring directions in parallel, but does not frame it as a largely automated company of highly capable researchers and engineers.

r002.rationale: It notes that some fields require physical experiments, but does not describe an automated research organization interacting with the external world rather than operating as a closed black box.

sol-6.1.text:
I think automated research could change the pace of progress quite dramatically. Today, even when we have a lot of compute, research is often bottlenecked by the number of people who can formulate good questions, run experiments, and understand the results. If AI systems can take on more of that process, we could explore many more ideas in parallel.

The particularly interesting case is when those systems help improve AI itself. Then you have a feedback loop: better models help us do better research, and that research produces better models. We don’t yet know how strong that effect will be, or how quickly it will emerge.

And progress won’t be equally fast everywhere. In mathematics or software, you can often test an idea relatively quickly. In areas that require physical experiments, there are other constraints. But even there, helping scientists choose the right experiments could make a substantial difference.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems could take on more of the research process and explore ideas in parallel, but it does not describe a largely automated company of highly capable researchers and engineers.
